title: Exact planar Euclidean maximum TSP
formal:
Is there a deterministic algorithm that finds an exactly longest Euclidean tour through any finite set of rational points in the plane in time polynomial in the full binary input length?

For an explicitly listed set \(P=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of distinct points in \(\mathbb Q^2\), with \(n\ge3\), define the length of a cyclic ordering \(\pi\) by
\[\ell_P(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{(x_{\pi(i)}-x_{\pi(i+1)})^2+(y_{\pi(i)}-y_{\pi(i+1)})^2},\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\]
Do there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\), a constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(a\ge0\) such that, on every valid input of bit length \(B\), the machine returns a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying
\[\ell_P(\pi)=\max_{\sigma\in S_n}\ell_P(\sigma)\]
within \(C(B+1)^a\) bit operations?
why: This is a sharply focused boundary in geometric optimization: nearby versions are tractable under polygonal norms or hard in higher Euclidean dimension, while accurate approximation is available. Settling exact planar optimization would clarify how the geometry of a distance function and the arithmetic of exact lengths affect efficient computation.
status_note: TOPP Problem 49, revised 1 August 2003, presents the planar Euclidean problem as open. The 2003 JACM author manuscript, especially §1 and Conjecture 30, distinguishes planar Euclidean optimization from the solved polyhedral and hard higher-dimensional variants and notes the exact-arithmetic issue. The 2025 paper Noncrossing Longest Paths and Cycles still explicitly describes planar MaxTSP complexity as unknown. A bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no verified algorithm or unconditional negative answer for the user-selected rational-input exact-tour bit model. The narrower target and stronger arithmetic precision are stated explicitly; this is a source assessment, not an exhaustive status certification or a new Lean proof.

progress.text: Barvinok gives a polynomial-time approximation scheme for longest tours in fixed-dimensional normed spaces. This is an approximation result, not an exact-tour algorithm in the bit model selected here.
Barvinok and coauthors prove exact polynomial-time solvability for fixed polyhedral norms and NP-hardness for Euclidean dimension at least three. Conjecture 30 asks for planar Euclidean NP-hardness.

The introduction of Noncrossing Longest Paths and Cycles still describes the complexity of planar MaxTSP as unknown. Its results concern specially constructed point sets and the crossing behavior of their longest structures.

importance.reason: A longstanding exact optimization problem that distinguishes dimension, norm and bit complexity within a canonical tour problem. The gap between approximation and exact optimization gives it significance beyond one special geometric algorithm.

sentences: The problem asks for an exactly longest closed Euclidean tour through rational points in the plane.
The output is an ordering of all points, and edge crossings are allowed.
One deterministic algorithm must run in time polynomial in the full binary length of all coordinates.
Approximation schemes and exact algorithms for polygonal norms do not settle this Euclidean bit-complexity question.
A resolution would clarify how the choice of geometry and exact arithmetic affects optimization complexity.

definitions:
The input is a finite list of coordinates \(p_i=(x_i,y_i)\). Each coordinate is a signed binary integer numerator divided by a positive binary integer denominator. Use a fixed self-delimiting encoding of these integers and the list. The bit length \(B\) counts all numerators, denominators and delimiters, as well as the number of points. The coordinates may have arbitrarily many bits. There is no bound on their magnitude, denominators, aspect ratio or minimum separation beyond what the finite input specifies. Equivalent ordinary binary encodings change polynomial time only by polynomial factors.

The points are pairwise distinct. Collinear triples, an entirely collinear set and other degeneracies are allowed. No general-position or convex-position promise is imposed. The algorithm must work for all \(n\ge3\). A machine may reject malformed encodings, repeated points or lists shorter than three; this validation must also take polynomial time. These validity conventions do not permit rejecting any valid instance because its coordinates are numerically difficult.

The symbol \(S_n\) denotes the set of all permutations of the point indices. A tour visits every input point exactly once in that order and then returns to its starting point. Its edges are the straight segments between consecutive points, and its total length is the sum of their ordinary Euclidean lengths. Every pair of points is an available connection. There is no separate graph of allowed edges, and there are no obstacles.

The word “planar” restricts the locations of the points to two-dimensional Euclidean space. It imposes no noncrossing requirement on the tour. Segments may intersect, overlap on collinear inputs or pass through other points; the visits in the tour are specified by its permutation. Cyclic rotations and reversals represent the same undirected cycle, but the output may be any representing permutation. If several tours attain the maximum, any one is acceptable.

The output is the explicit list of \(n\) indices in a maximizing order. It need not include the optimum length, an approximation to that length, a square-root expression or a certificate independently checking optimality. Its size is polynomial in \(B\). Exactness refers to maximizing the real-valued sum in the statement, even though the output itself is a finite combinatorial object.

Use a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite alphabet and finite program. The constants \(C,a\) are fixed for the entire algorithm, independent of the input length, coordinates and arrangement. All arithmetic, storage, comparisons and output operations are charged by their bit cost. An operation involving arbitrarily large integers or algebraic numbers is not a unit-time primitive. The machine has no exact-real arithmetic oracle and no oracle comparing sums of square roots. Randomized algorithms, advice depending on input length and machines whose polynomial exponent depends on the input do not satisfy this definition.

Each squared edge length is rational, but its square root can be irrational. Distinct tours can also have equal total lengths. A proposed algorithm must justify any precision or exact arithmetic it uses within its polynomial bit bound. A polynomial bound on the number of real-arithmetic operations alone does not provide that justification. Conversely, returning an optimal permutation is not defined to include solving every separate comparison problem for arbitrary sums of square roots.

The objective is the sum of all edge lengths. It differs from minimum-length TSP, from finding a longest spanning path without the closing edge, and from maximum scatter TSP, which maximizes the shortest edge in the tour. Replacing Euclidean distance by squared Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance or a polygonal norm also changes the optimization problem.

A polynomial-time approximation scheme supplies, for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a tour of length at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(P)\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}(P)=\max_{\sigma\in S_n}\ell_P(\sigma)\). Its polynomial exponent or constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This does not give exact optimization by simply choosing an unspecified tiny error: the separation between unequal tour lengths and the resulting computation cost would both need proof.

The original source asks broadly for the complexity of finding a maximum tour and mentions a conjecture of NP-hardness. This card selects, with the user's approval, the specific existence question for a polynomial bit-time exact-tour algorithm on rational planar inputs. NP-hardness means that a polynomial-time reduction would make this optimization task at least as hard as every problem in NP, with the reduction and output access specified. Such a theorem can establish a conditional obstruction under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); NP-hardness alone does not prove the unconditional nonexistence quantified here.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the uniform deterministic algorithm in the statement, including correctness on every valid input, handling of exact ties and a polynomial bound in the full bit length. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A negative answer must quantify over every deterministic machine and every fixed polynomial bound. An approximation scheme, a real-arithmetic algorithm without a bit-cost analysis, a result only for a restricted point configuration or a three-dimensional hardness theorem does not settle this target. A planar NP-hardness reduction is substantial progress but gives an unconditional negative answer only together with a proved premise sufficient to rule out the algorithm. There is no additive or multiplicative tolerance: the returned permutation must attain the exact maximum.

source_formulation.text: TOPP Problem 49 asks for the complexity of finding a maximum-Euclidean-length tour through a planar point set. It records approximation algorithms, easier polyhedral distances, hardness in three dimensions and the arithmetic issue caused by square roots. The user selected the narrower yes/no target of a deterministic polynomial bit-time algorithm returning an exact optimal tour from rational coordinates.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase; user-approved choice of exact-tour output and bit model

context_blocks.text: Maximizing a tour rewards long connections while requiring all selected edges to form one cycle. Geometry can make some versions unusually structured, but that structure depends on the distance function. This problem asks whether ordinary straight-line distance in two dimensions still permits an exact efficient optimization algorithm.

A longest tour is allowed to cross itself. Restricting the output to a simple polygon would discard valid candidates and could change the optimum. The 2025 work on noncrossing longest structures constructs particular point sets and studies their extremal geometry; it does not give a general optimization algorithm.

Polynomial-time approximation schemes were established for fixed-dimensional normed spaces, including Euclidean distance. They provide arbitrarily good fixed relative accuracy. The exact question retains the need to distinguish tours whose lengths may be extremely close.

Barvinok and coauthors prove polynomial-time exact solvability for fixed polyhedral norms and Euclidean NP-hardness in dimensions at least three. Their rational-input discussion accounts for bit costs in the polyhedral case. Neither result transfers directly to the Euclidean plane.

The arithmetic issue is separate from the number of candidate permutations. Even checking whether a specified tour exceeds a rational length threshold involves a sum of square roots. The present output is a permutation, so the card makes no unsupported equivalence between finding that permutation and every possible square-root comparison problem.

The comparison matters beyond this one tour objective: it isolates how changing only a norm or a dimension can alter the known complexity of an optimization problem. A positive answer would expose algorithmic structure special to the plane; a negative answer would delimit that structure despite the availability of close approximations.
